notes:
I've written the notes for 2 Chronicles 35 below. Each point gives the page URL and cites what that page says. A few limits on what I found:

- **Thin verses.** Verses 4–5 and 8–9 have little material, and I couldn't get a full verse-by-verse page from Gill, Ellicott or the Pulpit Commentary for verses 11–14.
- **Tradition differences.** The real disagreements (the ark in v. 3, whether Josiah sinned in v. 22, how Huldah's "in peace" promise came true) are between individual writers, not along denominational lines. I've given each writer's tradition where the site names it.
- **Not found.** I found nothing from Catholic or Orthodox sites (newadvent, catholic.com, oca.org), no bibleodyssey material, and no prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter.

---

## Part 1: Josiah's Passover (vv. 1–19)

**v. 1**
- Hezekiah's earlier Passover had to be held in the second month. Josiah was able to keep this great Passover at the appointed time in the first month (Numbers 9:1-5). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-35/
- Precept Austin says "in Jerusalem" marks the place God had chosen. It describes Josiah as running worship "by the book," and links the lamb to 1 Cor 5:7 ("Christ our Passover"). — https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-35-commentary
- Precept Austin also quotes Martin Selman: because the Passover comes right after the covenant renewal, it belongs to that renewal. Chronicles gives the reform a more positive face than Kings, which focuses on the campaign against idols. — same URL

**v. 2**
- Guzik quotes Spurgeon: first put every man in his proper place, then give each a good spirit for his work. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-35/

**v. 3 (the ark: a debated verse)**
- **Removed by wicked kings.** Ellicott says the command implies that the ark had been removed from its place in the inner sanctuary. The removal probably took place under Manasseh or his son, with the object of saving the sacred symbol from profanation. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/35-3.htm
- **Removed for repairs.** Barnes (Presbyterian) suggests it may have been temporarily removed from the holy of holies while Josiah effected necessary repairs. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-chronicles/35-3.html
- **Hidden by priests for safety.** Clarke (Wesleyan) thinks the priests had hidden it to protect it from idolatrous kings. Now that things were settled, it was ordered back to its own place. — same URL
- **Moved by Josiah.** Gill (Baptist) rejects the other options. He thinks Josiah himself had it moved during repairs of the most holy place. — same URL
- **Never removed (Keil's view).** Some read the verse as "leave the ark where it is; your carrying days are over." Ellicott calls this reading too artificial. The Restoration Commentary points to 2 Chr 5:7 and says nothing shows the ark had ever been taken out. It prefers Moffatt's rendering: since the ark is already in the temple, attend to worship. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/onr/2-chronicles-35.html
- **Jewish tradition.** Trapp reports a Hebrew tradition: priests carried the ark to the house of Shallum, Huldah's husband, during the idolatrous years. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jtc/2-chronicles-35.html
- **Application.** The Pulpit homily (Clarkson) says the Levites were to give up a lower, mechanical service for a higher, more spiritual one. — https://biblehub.com/sermons/2_chronicles/35-3.htm
- **Geneva note.** The Levites' charge included teaching the people God's word, not only temple work. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/35-3.htm

**vv. 4–6**
- Precept Austin says Josiah's instructions show that real reform is ordered by God's revealed pattern, not random. It adds that genuine ministry serves others, not self. "According to the word of the LORD by Moses" shows Josiah following God's instructions. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-35-commentary

**v. 7**
- Guzik calls the king's gift staggering generosity. He quotes Selman: the total offerings were more than double Hezekiah's. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-35/
- Precept Austin quotes Matthew Henry: It is to be feared that the congregation generally had not come provided; so that, if Josiah had not furnished them, the work of God must have stood still. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-35-commentary

**vv. 8–9**
- Guzik: the leader's generosity prompted the officials to give as well. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-35/

**v. 10**
- Guzik quotes Selman: "the service was prepared" is a rare phrase meaning everything was done as God required. — same URL

**v. 11 (who killed the lambs)**
- Selman (quoted by Guzik) says that, unlike Hezekiah's practice and the Pentateuch's implications, the Levites slaughtered all the lambs. Clarke instead suggests the people killed their own lambs and handed the blood to the priests. — same URL

**vv. 12–13**
- Trapp, quoted by Guzik, reads the roasting as a picture of Christ "roasted" in the fire of the Father's wrath. Payne says the cattle served as peace offerings for the week of Unleavened Bread. — same URL

**v. 14**
- Guzik: the order was right. The people were served first, then the priests and Levites. — same URL

**v. 15**
- Guzik says the Law of Moses did not prescribe singing at Passover, so Josiah went beyond the command. The gatekeepers stayed at their posts, a sign he kept the kingdom secure. — same URL

**vv. 16–17**
- Guzik: everything was done "the same day" to obey the Mosaic date. — same URL

**v. 18 ("no such Passover since Samuel")**
- **What made it unique:**
  - Exact obedience. Matthew Henry (quoted by Precept Austin) says it was done with great exactness according to the law, while Hezekiah's Passover had irregularities. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-35-commentary
  - Devotion and strict adherence to the Law. JFB says it was not the grandeur or the size of the crowd but the ardent devotion of the king and people, the disregard of purely traditional customs, and the unusually strict adherence to the Law. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/35-18.htm
  - Generosity. Clarke (Wesleyan) quotes Calmet: Josiah gave out more animals than David or Solomon did. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-chronicles/35-18.html
- **The people's heart (a dissenting note).** Matthew Henry says that, unlike at Hezekiah's Passover, the people kept it more in compliance with the king than from real desire. — same URL
- **"Samuel" vs. "the judges."** Kings says "since the judges"; JFB says this means the same, because Samuel ended the era of the judges. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/35-18.htm
- **"Kings of Israel."** Precept Austin takes this to mean the whole nation, including David and Solomon. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-35-commentary
- **Reformed (Ligonier).** The Chronicler's first readers were exiles back from Babylon. They needed encouragement to eagerly and lavishly celebrate the appointed feast of Passover. — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/josiahs-passover
- **Modern scholarship.** Sara Japhet (quoted by Precept Austin) sees Hezekiah's Passover as a spontaneous effort to bring in northerners. Josiah's, by contrast, set up a permanent institution with clear roles and a firm legal basis. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-35-commentary

**v. 19**
- Keil: the eighteenth-year date points back to 34:8 and shows that Josiah's cultus reform culminated in this passover. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/35-18.htm

## Part 2: Josiah's Death (vv. 20–27)

**v. 20**
- Guzik places this in the struggle between declining Assyria and rising Babylon, with Egypt allied to Assyria. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-35/
- The Restoration Commentary says mentioning the temple work is only for dating. It shows the disaster did not undo the king's life work. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/onr/2-chronicles-35.html

**v. 21 (Neco's "God told me")**
- **Unknowing prophecy.** Guzik says Neco probably meant his own gods. Nevertheless, it was an unknowing divine prophecy, much as the words of Caiaphas regarding the death of Jesus (John 11:49-52). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-35/
- **Pagan boast, finger of God.** The Pulpit Commentary compares Neco's words to claims of divine command by earlier Egyptian kings. Still, it is nevertheless clear that the Chronicler beheld in the incident the finger of God. — https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-35.html
- **God could speak through him.** Precept Austin says nothing stopped God speaking through Neco, as with Balaam's donkey and Cyrus. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-35-commentary
- **Commentators disagree.** Ellicott says they are split: either it was a real commission (perhaps through Jeremiah), or Neco used God's name as an authority Josiah would respect. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/35-22.htm
- **Modern scholarship (Myers, Anchor Bible).** Coffman reports Myers' citation of 1 Esdras 1:27 for the claim that the warning came from Jeremiah. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/2-chronicles-35.html
  - The Restoration Commentary says it could not find that statement in 1 Esdras. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/onr/2-chronicles-35.html

**v. 22 (how far Josiah was to blame)**
- **Blame is clear (MacArthur, Baptist / gty.org).** Josiah had not sought God's counsel on whether to fight. Nonetheless, God gave His counsel through Josiah's pagan opponent. — https://www.gty.org/blogs/B160701/josiah-and-picking-the-wrong-fight
- **Stubborn pride (Guzik, enduringword).** Guzik also quotes Knapp: the disguise and the lack of any recorded prayer show it was "not of faith." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-35/
- **A softer view (Poole).** If Josiah sinned, it was only a sin of ignorance. Still, he should have asked God and cannot be wholly excused. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/35-22.htm
- **A weakness (Gill, Baptist).** Gill calls it an "infirmity": Josiah did not believe the words came from the Lord and did not inquire. — same URL
- **No condemnation in Scripture (Pulpit Commentary).** It says No condemnation of Josiah's conduct is written on the page of Scripture in connection with this. — https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-35.html
- **Rashness, not wrong opposition (Matthew Henry).** Henry says Scripture does not condemn Josiah for opposing Pharaoh. His fault was not inquiring of the Lord. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/35-25.htm
- **Wrong politics (G. Campbell Morgan, quoted by Guzik).** Josiah had no business supporting Assyria; the prophets kept warning kings against such alliances. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-35/
- **Misread promise (Poole).** Poole suggests Josiah may have misread Huldah's promise (34:28) as a guarantee of safety. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/35-22.htm
- **"Disguised himself."**
  - The Pulpit Commentary thinks it more likely means "fully armed himself"; the Septuagint has "strengthened himself." — same URL
  - Ellicott rejects Keil's figurative reading ("departed from his true character"). — same URL

**v. 23**
- The Pulpit homily: whether or not the Egyptian archers saw through the disguise, Jehovah did. — https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-35.html
- Precept Austin: the sovereign God guided the arrow to fulfil the warning. One bad decision can have huge consequences. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-35-commentary

**v. 24 (and Huldah's "in peace")**
- **Where he died.** Keil says Chronicles does not state where he died. Comparing Zech 12:11, Keil thinks he probably died on the way. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-kings/23-1.html
- **Promise kept by death in Jerusalem (Clarke).** Clarke argues he was wounded at Megiddo but died in peace in Jerusalem, so Huldah's word held. — https://studylight.org/bible/hnv/2-kings/22-20.html
- **Promise kept by timing (Barnes).** Barnes calls the death a verbal contradiction to this prophecy, but not in real opposition to its spirit. Josiah died before the Babylonian disaster came. — same URL
- **Three senses (Guzik).** Guzik gives three ways the promise was true: Josiah died before the exile, was gathered to his fathers in peace, and died in God's favour. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-22/

**v. 25**
- **Not our Book of Lamentations.** Ellicott says the dirges were collected in a separate "Book of Dirges." This was quite different from the canonical book of Lamentations. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/35-25.htm
- **Lam 4:20.** Gill says that verse refers to Zedekiah, and Jeremiah's lament is lost. — same URL
  - Easton's dictionary instead links Lam 4:20 to Josiah. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/search/Dictionary/viewTopic.cfm?topic=ET0002116
- **Lost, or part of Lamentations.** Barnes reports that some find the lament in all or part of Lamentations, but most think it is lost. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/35-25.htm
- **Annual mourning.** Gill cites the Targum and Jarchi (Rashi): there was a yearly mourning, which Jarchi places on the ninth of Ab. — same URL
- **A proverb of grief.** JFB says the "lamentation of Hadad-rimmon" (Zech 12:11) became a byword for great sorrow. — same URL
- **Septuagint reading.** The Septuagint reads "ruling men and women" instead of "singing men and women." — same URL
- **Moral lesson (Matthew Henry).** Those who mourned Josiah may not have been thankful for him while he lived. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Ch/2Ch_035.cfm

**vv. 26–27**
- Kingcomments notes the Chronicler ends with Josiah's "deeds of devotion," not his failure. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/2-chronicles-35.html
- Precept Austin explains the word as *ḥesed*: covenant loyalty that mirrored God's own steadfast love. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-35-commentary
